title: Best Cordless Drills UK
short: Drill drivers, combi drills, hammer drills and SDS drills compared by power, torque and battery life, for everyday DIY to heavy-duty jobs.
intro: The right cordless drill depends on the job: a light drill driver suits flat-pack furniture, while masonry or concrete needs a hammer or SDS drill. This guide compares drills tested by Expert Reviews across softwood, hardwood, brick and concrete, with a screwdriving test on every model.

products.name: UniversalImpact 18V
products.best_for: Buyers who want one do-it-all drill
products.summary: Expert Reviews' Best Buy, taking on everything from driving screws into softwood to Rawlplug holes in brick, only slowing down (but still succeeding) in tough concrete. The keyless chuck locks bits securely, and the standard 18V Power-4-All battery charges in about an hour.
pros: Handles nearly any household drilling or screwdriving task
Clever keyless chuck design
Widely available for under £100
Compatible with Bosch's wider 18V tool range
cons: Struggles (though still succeeds) in tough concrete
Slightly heavier than the lightest combi drills

products.name: DHP458Z
products.best_for: Buyers tackling more demanding or frequent DIY work
products.summary: Gives pro-level features at a reasonable price, speeding through softwood, hardwood and brick, with even concrete not holding it off for long in Expert Reviews' testing. A sliding side grip with a depth rod adds control, though it's a relatively heavy, loud tool.
pros: Strong performance across wood, brick and concrete
Adjustable side grip with depth-stop rod
Efficient keyless chuck grips slender bits well
Well-balanced despite its weight
cons: Noisy in use, especially on hammer mode

products.name: 13 Piece 18V Cordless Drill Driver
products.best_for: Light repairs and flat-pack furniture on a tight budget
products.summary: A cheap drill that comes with six drill bits, six screwdriver bits and an adaptor, doing a great job on basic household needs and light repairs in Expert Reviews' testing. It isn't powerful enough for metal or brickwork, and the battery is slow to charge and modest in capacity.
pros: Very cheap, ready to use out of the box
Generous bundled bit set
Lightweight and versatile for basic tasks
cons: Not powerful enough for metal or brickwork

products.name: UniversalDrill 18V
products.best_for: Buyers who want a quiet, reliable all-rounder without an impact function
products.summary: A reliable all-rounder that Expert Reviews measured at just 72dB drilling into concrete, notably quieter than rivals, with minimal vibration and a comfortable one-handed grip. It struggles with solid concrete or thick screws, where a hammer or impact drill would do better.
pros: Notably quiet in use
Comfortable, well-balanced, low vibration
Two-speed gearbox suits both screws and fast drilling
cons: Struggles with solid concrete or thick screws
The similarly-priced UniversalImpact offers more versatility

products.name: CLX228AJ
products.best_for: Buyers who want a combi drill and impact driver in one kit
products.key_spec: 12V Max, combi drill + impact driver, batteries and charger included
products.summary: Bundles a combi drill and an impact driver with batteries and a charger in one case, covering most DIY needs short of boring large holes through brick or concrete. Expert Reviews found both tools solidly built with LED lights, though the combi drill can be loud in use.
pros: Combi drill and impact driver in one kit
Both tools solidly built with LED lights
No corners cut for the price
cons: Combi drill can be loud in use
Not intended for large holes in brick or concrete

products.name: 18V Cordless 2-Gear Combi Hammer Drill
products.best_for: Buyers who occasionally need light masonry or metalwork
products.summary: A terrific all-rounder for household jobs that's also tough enough for light masonry and metalwork thanks to its high hammer-drilling speed. Expert Reviews notes the battery holds 80% of its charge over 90 days, though for the most heavy-duty tasks a proper rotary hammer drill is still recommended.
pros: Good value for a hammer-function drill
Handles light masonry and metalwork
Battery retains charge well over time
cons: Not intended for the most heavy-duty masonry jobs

products.name: WX354 SlammerDrill
products.best_for: Buyers who want extra hammer-drilling power without a full SDS drill
products.summary: Punches above its weight with a hammer action that easily puts holes into brick or concrete, and effortless performance on wood, in Expert Reviews' tests. It comes bundled with two batteries and a charger, which helps justify a price that otherwise looks steep for its size.
pros: Strong hammer action for brick and concrete
Effortless on wood, with plenty of control
Comes bundled with two batteries and a charger
cons: Pricier than its size might suggest

products.name: 18V XR Lithium-Ion SDS
products.best_for: Regular, heavy-duty work through masonry, concrete or steel
products.summary: A surprisingly powerful SDS drill for its size, packing corded-level power into a 3kg tool. Expert Reviews found low vibration levels made long sessions easier on the arm, with a useful hammer-only mode not found on cheaper models, though it isn't intended for occasional DIYers.
pros: Corded-level power in a lightweight, portable tool
Low vibration for long drilling sessions
Useful hammer-only mode
cons: Overkill and pricier than needed for occasional DIY

products.name: One+ R18IDBL
products.best_for: Driving lots of screws quickly, including decking
products.key_spec: 18V brushless, up to 270Nm torque, DeckDrive mode
products.summary: Delivers huge torque that drove screws through decking with barely any effort in Expert Reviews' testing, including a specialised DeckDrive mode that slows down as the screw head nears the surface to avoid splitting. It's heavier than a standard combi drill once fitted with a battery, and isn't designed to drill holes.
pros: Huge torque for driving screws and loosening stuck bolts
DeckDrive mode avoids splitting timber
Three power levels for precise control
cons: Heavier than a standard combi drill once battery is fitted

guide.q: Do I need a combi drill, drill driver or impact driver?
guide.a: A basic drill driver suits light drilling and screwdriving around the home. A combi drill adds a hammer function for masonry, making it the most versatile all-rounder. An impact driver, like the Ryobi here, is a specialist tool for driving screws quickly and shouldn't be used for drilling precise holes.

guide.q: When do I need a hammer drill or SDS drill instead of a combi drill?
guide.a: A combi drill's hammer function handles occasional light masonry work fine. If you're regularly drilling into brick, concrete or stone, a dedicated hammer drill or, for the toughest jobs, an SDS rotary hammer like the DeWalt here will get through faster and with less strain on the tool.

guide.q: How much battery capacity (Ah) do I actually need?
guide.a: A smaller battery (1.5-2Ah) is lighter and fine for occasional use around the home. A larger battery (4Ah and above) lasts longer between charges and suits frequent use or bigger projects, though it adds weight to the tool.

guide.q: Does it matter if I already own batteries from a brand's tool range?
guide.a: Yes, it's worth checking first. Buying a bare tool (no battery) from a brand whose batteries you already own, such as Bosch's Power-4-All or DeWalt's XR range, can save a significant amount versus buying a drill with batteries and charger included.
